blocks.text: A halogenoalkane, R-X, has two parts: an alkyl group with a partial positive charge on the carbon attached to the halogen, and the halogen atom with a partial negative charge. Experiments show that the strength of the carbon-halogen bond is the main factor deciding the reactivity: the weaker the bond, the more easily it breaks and the more reactive the molecule.

blocks.caption: Bond energies of C-X bonds (book's Table 21.1)

blocks.text: Iodo compounds, with the weakest bonds, are the most reactive and fluoro compounds the least: R-I > R-Br > R-Cl > R-F. The C-F bond is so strong that fluoroalkanes do not react under ordinary conditions. Other factors, such as bond polarity, steric hindrance and inductive effects, can also affect reactivity.

blocks.prompt: Why are fluoroalkanes rarely attacked by nucleophiles?
blocks.explanation: The C-F bond is the strongest carbon-halogen bond (467 kJ/mol in Table 21.1), so it is very hard to break.

items: Reactivity is decided mainly by C-X bond strength.
R-I > R-Br > R-Cl > R-F; fluoroalkanes are unreactive.
